title: Flood Fill
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated full-grid scans until no changes versus a single DFS/BFS spread.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an image grid, a starting pixel (sr, sc), and a new color, perform a flood fill: recolor the starting pixel and every pixel connected to it (4-directionally) that shares the STARTING pixel's original color.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Recolor a connected region starting from a pixel, like a paint bucket tool\"","A classic flood-fill DFS/BFS: spread outward from the starting cell to every 4-directionally adjacent cell sharing the same original value"]]}

blocks.text: Starting from (sr, sc), a DFS (or BFS) spreads to every 4-directionally adjacent pixel that still has the STARTING pixel's ORIGINAL color, recoloring each one visited. The search naturally stops at pixels of a different color, since they are not part of the connected region to be recolored.

blocks.title: Analogy: Using a Paint Bucket Tool in an Image Editor
blocks.text: Picture clicking a paint bucket tool on a pixel in an image editor: the tool spreads outward, recoloring every directly touching pixel that shared the original color, stopping wherever a different color is encountered.

blocks.caption: DFS/BFS from the start pixel, spreading to same-colored 4-directional neighbors

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Record the STARTING pixel's original color BEFORE any recoloring begins, since it will be needed as the reference throughout the search.

Observation 2: If the new color equals the original color, no work is needed at all (recoloring to the same color would otherwise cause infinite recursion).

Observation 3: A DFS (or BFS) from the starting pixel, recoloring each visited pixel and spreading only to 4-directionally adjacent pixels STILL matching the original color, correctly reaches the entire connected region exactly once.
This leads to a straightforward DFS (or BFS) from the starting pixel, recoloring and spreading to same-original-colored neighbors.
Repeatedly scan the entire image, recoloring any pixel adjacent to an already-recolored pixel that still matches the original color, looping until a full scan makes no further changes.
Why the code is written this way

items: Repeatedly scanning until no changes occur eventually recolors the correct region.
This costs many redundant full-grid scans; a single DFS/BFS spread directly from the starting pixel visits exactly the connected region once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((rows times cols) squared) worst case, due to repeated full scans.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the image itself.
Limitation: a single DFS or BFS starting from the given pixel visits exactly the connected region once, without any repeated scanning.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Record the original color at (sr, sc). If it already equals the new color, return immediately (avoiding infinite recursion). Otherwise, run a DFS (or BFS) from (sr, sc): recolor the current pixel, then recurse into each of its four neighbors, but only if that neighbor is within bounds AND still matches the original color.
Use a single DFS (or BFS) from the starting pixel, recoloring and spreading to same-original-colored neighbors exactly once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["Start at (1,1), original color 1","Recolor to 2, spread to neighbors"],["(0,1), (1,0), (2,1) etc.","Recolored if still color 1, spread continues"],["(1,2) is color 0","Not recolored, search stops there"]]}

blocks.text: Recording the original color once before any recoloring begins, and checking against it (not the new color) at every step, correctly identifies exactly the connected region of the starting pixel's ORIGINAL color; the DFS naturally visits each pixel in that region exactly once, since once recolored, a pixel no longer matches the original color and further recursive calls into it stop immediately.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times cols), each pixel visited at most once.
Space: O(rows times cols) recursion depth worst case.

blocks.text: Flood Fill is the foundational grid connectivity problem, directly modeling a paint bucket tool via DFS or BFS.

items: Forgetting to check if the new color equals the original color first, causing infinite recursion when they match.
Comparing against the NEW color instead of the ORIGINAL color when deciding whether to spread further.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "check the new color against the original color first, to avoid infinite recursion" heads off the most common bug in this problem immediately.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "recolor a connected region like a paint bucket tool", think: DFS or BFS spreading from the starting cell to same-colored neighbors.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The repeated-scanning brute force costs O((rows times cols) squared) worst case; the single DFS/BFS spread costs O(rows times cols), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: DFS or BFS grid flood fill, spreading from a starting cell.
Core Idea: recolor the starting pixel and every 4-directionally connected pixel sharing its ORIGINAL color.
Time: O((rows times cols)^2) worst case for the brute force, O(rows times cols) for the DFS/BFS approach.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(rows times cols) recursion depth for the DFS/BFS approach.
Most Important Observation: checking the new color against the original color first avoids infinite recursion.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy grid DFS/BFS problem.
One line memory trick: spread to same-colored neighbors, recolor as you go.
